anchors.fact: By the late 1930s he had wealth and some fame beyond Cuba, yet each morning he still put on the white jacket and went behind the bar to mix drinks (Oxford pdf 1655; F7). This ran until 1950, when ill health took him from behind the bar (pdf 1657; F12): never "to the end".
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted: he kept choosing the working side when he no longer needed to. Whether the jacket or the famous man was the disguise is the bartender's question, not the record's.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls him plain to look at, quiet and reserved in manner (pdf 1655; F6).
anchors.meaning: The ordinary side is on the page. Paraphrase only.

anchors.fact: He squeezed every lime by hand, fingers only, and in the same sentence was a pioneer of electric mixers (pdf 1655–1656; F8).
anchors.meaning: Plain handwork, kept by choice beside the newest tools, not a refusal of them.

anchors.fact: He told an American journalist in 1935 that he made up a new drink every day, as self-discipline (pdf 1656; F9). His words, through the journalist.
anchors.meaning: Keeping the edge daily: the fear of going weak, answered in his own words. Never "hours" or "in secret".

anchors.fact: He bought the bar in 1935, and by the late 1930s was rich and known abroad (pdf 1655; F5, F7).
anchors.meaning: A setting only. No "king", no superlative (C3), no famous customers.

anchors.fact: Oxford counts the Floridita (rum, red vermouth, white crème de cacao, lime, a little orange curaçao and grenadine) among his lasting creations (pdf 1656, 821; F10, F13).
anchors.meaning: His, on two entries. Oxford's recipe cites only Vic's 1972 guide and is in no booklet of his, so never "his recipe".

anchors.fact: For reasons nobody knows, it isn't in any of the souvenir recipe booklets he put out for the bar (pdf 821; F14), though he did reprint praise of himself in them (*Imbibe!* pdf 216; F17). No booklet years (C2).
anchors.meaning: The one thing of his that wasn't put forward. Any why is "I like to think". Never "he left it out".

anchors.fact: Trader Vic came across it on a visit in 1938, put it on the first menu of his own restaurant, and later printed it in his bar guide; Oxford's writer says it would have been lost otherwise (pdf 821; F15).
anchors.meaning: The part never put forward is the part someone else carried home: the answer to "would they still call?". One clause, owned; no leg, no shark, no Mai Tai, no "loved".

cocktail.closingLine: Half the lime, squeezed by hand. When you're next introduced, bring up something the introduction doesn't cover.
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
Before you cut the lime, take one wide strip of peel off it with a vegetable peeler, green only, none of the white underneath. Set it aside.
Cut the lime in half. Squeeze one half over a jigger with your fingers, nothing else, until you have 15 ml.
Put the rum, vermouth, crème de cacao, curaçao, grenadine and lime juice in a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain it into the cold glass.
Hold the strip of peel over the drink, green side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Lay it on the rim.
cocktail.name: Day Job

recipe.item: white rum, Cuban style (light and dry, unaged or lightly aged), 40% or stronger
recipe.note: the recipe asks for Cuban or Puerto Rican; below 40% the drink goes thin
clear as water, and it tastes of chocolate

recipe.item: fresh lime juice: half a lime, squeezed by hand
recipe.note: measure it: a whole lime makes the drink too sharp and too weak

recipe.item: wide strip of lime peel, cut from the same lime

cocktail.tagline: You could make the whole room feel slow. You never have.

reading.epigraph: Its first maker put out booklets of the bar's drinks. This one's in none of them.
whoYouAre: Most days you're easy to miss: quiet in a meeting, with a joke that lands a second too late. Then something turns up that only you can sort out, like a friend's figures that won't balance the night before they're due, or a letter that has to be exactly right. For an hour you're someone else entirely. Afterwards you go back to being easy to miss, and that part is on purpose. You'd rather nobody near you felt outshone.

Ask which of the two is the costume, and you'd hesitate. Years ago, without quite noticing, you decided the quiet one was the disguise, and the ability was the real you. So you keep it sharp, every day, because going rusty would feel like disappearing. The people you're with get someone who could make them feel small and chooses, every time, to make them feel capable instead. That's worth more to them than the ability.
yours: Constante Ribalaigua came to Havana from near Barcelona as a child. At sixteen, as he told it later, his father, a bartender himself, asked if he'd like to learn the trade, and he said yes. He made his name at La Florida, the Floridita. In 1935 he bought it, and by the end of that decade he was rich, and known abroad too. He's remembered as quiet and reserved, and not much to look at. And every morning he still put on the white jacket and went behind the bar to mix drinks.

He squeezed every lime by hand, with his fingers only, though he was one of the first to put electric mixers on a bar. He told a journalist in 1935 that he made up a new drink every day, "as self discipline". Among the drinks he created was the Floridita: rum, red vermouth, a little chocolate liqueur and lime. He put out booklets of the bar's recipes, and for reasons we don't know, that one isn't in any of them. A visiting bartender, Trader Vic, came across it in 1938, put it on the first menu of his own place, and printed it years later. Without him, it might have been lost.

I like to think the jacket was the point: he no longer needed it, and he chose it anyway, morning after morning. I recognise you in that. You'd probably call the ability the real you. I'd call it the jacket: you put it on for other people. Who you are is the one who keeps choosing to. And of everything he made, one of the drinks that lasted is the one that isn't in any of his booklets.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Floridita, with two changes of my own. It's white rum, red vermouth, a little crème de cacao (a chocolate liqueur as clear as water), and grenadine and orange curaçao, one spoonful of each, shaken hard and strained into a slim stemmed glass that's been in the freezer. My first change is half a lime instead of a whole one, because a whole one makes it too sharp. Squeeze it with your fingers, the way he squeezed his limes. The second change is the twist: the lime's own peel instead of orange, so the lime that balances the drink scents it too. You'd only notice it if you knew, and that felt like you. It tastes of chocolate and lime, and it's a delicious one.

One thing to take with you. People will keep introducing you by what you can do: "this is the one who can sort anything out." When it happens again, let them, and then add something about you that has nothing to do with it: the song you can't stop playing, the town you'd move to tomorrow, something you're hopeless at. Watch which one they ask about. And let the quiet one be introduced too. It was never the disguise.
